questions.question: What is a problem with riding alongside another rider?

options.text: It wastes road space.
It limits your escape routes if something goes wrong.
It makes it harder to talk to the other rider.
It makes it easier for other cars to pass you.

questions.correctAnswerText: It limits your escape routes if something goes wrong.
questions.explanation: Do not ride alongside another motorcycle. If a hazard appears, you and the other rider will have fewer escape routes.

questions.question: When passing another vehicle, what must you do?

options.text: You can pass in a no passing zone.
You can go 10 mph over the speed limit.
Start and finish your pass in a passing zone only.
Pass on the shoulder if one exists.

questions.correctAnswerText: Start and finish your pass in a passing zone only.
questions.explanation: Only pass in areas where passing is safe and legal. Follow the posted speed limit and stay within the passing zone.

questions.question: If your motorcycle starts to wobble, what should you do?

options.text: Shift to a lower gear.
Speed up.
Hold the handlebars tight and slowly release the throttle.
Brake slowly.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold the handlebars tight and slowly release the throttle.
questions.explanation: Do not speed up, as this makes the wobble worse. Instead, grip the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle. Shift your weight forward and down. Get off the road as soon as possible. Do not brake, as this can make the wobble worse.

questions.question: When riding at night, what should you NOT do?

options.text: Slow down.
Keep more distance from other vehicles.
Use your high beam headlight.
Follow closely behind other vehicles.

questions.correctAnswerText: Follow closely behind other vehicles.
questions.explanation: At night, ride slower and stay farther away from other vehicles. Use the headlights of vehicles ahead to see the road better. Do not follow closely behind other vehicles.

questions.question: When riding behind a car, where should you position your motorcycle?

options.text: Where the driver can see you in their rearview mirror.
Assume the driver already sees you.
In the far left part of the lane.
In the far right part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Where the driver can see you in their rearview mirror.
questions.explanation: Position your motorcycle in the center of the lane. This way, the driver will see you in the middle of their rearview mirror, where they are most likely to notice you.

questions.question: When other drivers might try to squeeze into your lane, where should you ride?

options.text: Allow other riders to share your lane.
In the center of the lane.
In the right part of the lane.
On the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the center of the lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane in heavy traffic. This discourages other drivers from trying to squeeze in next to you. Lane sharing is illegal and unsafe in Maryland.

questions.question: Why should you avoid riding directly alongside another vehicle?

options.text: You can end up in the driver's blind spot.
It is safer than riding behind the vehicle.
It is safe because it reduces your escape routes.
You should only do it at night.

questions.correctAnswerText: You can end up in the driver's blind spot.
questions.explanation: Riding alongside another vehicle puts you in its blind spot. The driver may not see you and could turn into your lane. Also, the vehicle blocks your escape route if danger appears.

questions.question: If a small animal enters your lane while you are in traffic, what should you do?

options.text: Swerve into other lanes to avoid hitting it.
Switch lanes quickly.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to scare it away.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in your lane.
questions.explanation: Stay in your lane. Swerving into another lane to avoid a small animal risks hitting another car, which is more dangerous than hitting the animal.

questions.question: If your motorcycle starts to wobble, what should you do?

options.text: Brake slowly.
Speed up.
Hold the handlebars tight and slowly release the throttle.
Shift to a lower gear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold the handlebars tight and slowly release the throttle.
questions.explanation: Do not speed up, as this makes the wobble worse. Instead, grip the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle. Shift your weight forward and down. Get off the road as soon as possible. Do not brake, as this can make the wobble worse.

questions.question: Why should motorcycle riders not rely only on mirrors?

options.text: Motorcycle mirrors are smaller than car mirrors.
Motorcycles have blind spots, just like cars.
Mirrors are never accurate.
Mirrors take your eyes off the road and should not be used.

questions.correctAnswerText: Motorcycles have blind spots, just like cars.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles have blind spots. You cannot rely only on your mirrors to see what is behind you. Check over your shoulder often to see what is in your blind spots.

questions.question: To control your motorcycle well, you should:

options.text: Sit with your arms holding you up rather than steering.
Keep your knees against the gas tank for balance.
Let your feet hang off the footrests.
Sit far back so you must stretch to reach the handgrips.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your knees against the gas tank for balance.
questions.explanation: Keep your knees against the gas tank to help balance when turning. Sit so your arms can steer, not hold you up. Sit close enough that your arms bend slightly at the handgrips. Keep your feet firmly on the footrests.

questions.question: If you are riding behind a car, you should:

options.text: Stay in a lane position where the driver can see you.
Always ride in the far left part of the lane.
Not worry about where you position yourself.
Always ride in the far right part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in a lane position where the driver can see you.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane behind a car. This makes you most visible in the car's rearview mirror. Drivers check their rearview mirror more often than their side mirrors.

questions.question: When it starts raining, it is usually best to:

options.text: Ride in the center of the lane.
Pull off the road until the rain stops.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
Speed up.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: Do not ride down the center of a lane in wet weather. Ride in the tire tracks left by cars ahead of you. The left track is often best, but this depends on traffic and conditions.

questions.question: The center portion of a lane usually contains an oily strip. This part of the lane is:

options.text: Never safe for motorcyclists.
Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
Usually safe, unless it is sunny.
Always safe, no matter the weather.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in a strip down the center of traffic lanes. When the road is dry, this area usually has enough traction for motorcycles. The strip is usually about two feet wide, so you can often ride to one side and still be in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: When approaching a blind intersection with a stop sign, riders should:

options.text: Stop at the stop sign then go through the intersection.
Ignore the stop sign and move forward to see better.
Stop at the stop sign, then move forward slowly to see cross traffic better.
Go through the intersection without stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop at the stop sign, then move forward slowly to see cross traffic better.
questions.explanation: At a blind intersection with a stop sign, stop where marked. Then move forward slowly and stop again just before the crossroad. Lean forward and look around buildings, parked cars, or bushes to check for traffic. Keep your front wheel out of the crossroad while looking.

questions.question: When making a turn:

options.text: There is less traction available for stopping.
There is more traction available for stopping.
Stopping is the same as stopping on a straight road.
You should never try to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: There is less traction available for stopping.
questions.explanation: You can brake while turning, but use great care. When a motorcycle leans to turn, some traction is used for turning. This leaves less traction for braking.

questions.question: Which of the following is not protective clothing?

options.text: A leather jacket
Full-fingered gloves
Long pants made of denim
Athletic shoes

questions.correctAnswerText: Athletic shoes
questions.explanation: A leather jacket, full-fingered gloves, and long denim pants protect you in a fall. Wear lace-up boots, high-top boots, or heavy shoes that support your ankles.

questions.question: More than half of all crashes:

options.text: Happen at speeds greater than 35 mph.
Are caused by worn tires.
Happen in the dark.
Involve riders with little experience on their motorcycles.

questions.correctAnswerText: Involve riders with little experience on their motorcycles.
questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes involve riders with little experience on their motorcycles.

questions.question: When braking where traction is reduced, you should:

options.text: Apply the brakes faster than usual.
Apply the brakes more gently than usual.
Not use the rear brake.
Not use the front brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Apply the brakes more gently than usual.
questions.explanation: When slowing or stopping on a slippery surface, use caution and apply the brakes gently.

questions.question: When carrying a passenger or cargo:

options.text: It may take less time to accelerate, but more time to stop.
It may take more time to accelerate and stop.
It may take more time to accelerate, but less time to stop.
It may take less time to accelerate and stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: It may take more time to accelerate and stop.
questions.explanation: Extra weight from a passenger or cargo makes your motorcycle take longer to speed up and slow down.

questions.question: When passing parked cars on your right with no oncoming traffic, you should:

options.text: Stay toward the right side of your lane.
Stay toward the left side of your lane.
Look to your left frequently.
Use your rearview mirrors more often than usual.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay toward the left side of your lane.
questions.explanation: Stay on the side of your lane away from parked cars. This protects you from car doors opening or people stepping out. If traffic is coming toward you, stay in the center of your lane.

questions.question: When being passed, which of the following is NOT a hazard:

options.text: Extended mirrors.
Objects being thrown from other vehicles.
Blasts of wind.
Headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Headlights.
questions.explanation: When being passed, watch out for the vehicle's mirrors, wind from the passing vehicle, and objects that may be thrown. Headlights from a passing vehicle are not a hazard.

questions.question: To be more visible at an intersection, you should:

options.text: Turn your headlight off.
Ride with your headlight on.
Try to make eye contact with other drivers.
Ride as close as possible to the vehicle ahead.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride with your headlight on.
questions.explanation: The best way to be seen at an intersection is to ride with your headlight on. Keep your headlight on whenever your motorcycle is running.

questions.question: When riding at night, you should:

options.text: Adjust your lane position for changing conditions.
Travel faster than usual to reach your destination quicker.
Always use your low beam headlight to see better.
Stay as close as possible to the vehicle ahead.

questions.correctAnswerText: Adjust your lane position for changing conditions.
questions.explanation: Be flexible with your lane position when riding at night. Use safe riding strategies for poor visibility conditions.

questions.question: An effective eye or face shield should have all of the following qualities, except:

options.text: Free of scratches.
Resistant to penetration.
Able to fasten securely.
Airtight.

questions.correctAnswerText: Airtight.
questions.explanation: Good eye protection and face shields must be free of scratches, resist penetration, fasten securely, allow air to pass through, and fit over eyeglasses or sunglasses. They do not need to be airtight.
